1:
Henry takes the apostle to be reproving a very corrupt practice, one that seemed a growing evil in the churches even in those early ages, and has since sadly divided Christian societies. He draws three things out of the caution. The character of Christians is fully implied in it: they are such as have the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ — they embrace it, govern themselves by it, and hold it as a trust and as a treasure. Then, James speaks honourably of Christ in calling him the Lord of glory. And that title should teach us not to respect Christians for anything so much as their conformity to Christ: those who profess to believe the glory of our Lord Jesus, which the poorest Christian shall partake of equally with the rich, should not make men's outward advantages the measure of their respect. However lightly any may think of it, Henry insists, this is a heinous sin.

Calvin admits the reproof seems at first sight hard. It is a duty of courtesy to honour those elevated in the world; and if respect of persons be vicious, servants would have to be freed from all subjection, since freedom and servitude are reckoned by Paul among the conditions of life. But the difficulty vanishes if what James writes is not separated, for he does not disapprove of honour being paid to the rich, but of its being done in a way that despises the poor. Ambitious and full of vanity is that honour which is shown to the rich in contempt of the poor, and ambition reigns whenever the masks of this world are alone in high esteem. Read as though it said that he sins who respects the rich, the sentence would be absurd; read as saying that he sins who honours the rich alone and treats the poor with contempt, it is true doctrine. Calvin adds that respect of persons cannot be united with the faith of Christ, for we are by faith made one body in which Christ holds the primacy; when the pomps of the world grow so preeminent as to cover what Christ is, faith has little vigour in us.

The grammarians take up the two disputed phrases. Robertson makes the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ clearly an objective genitive — faith in him, as in the command to have faith in God — and notes that the imperative with the negative exhorts them to stop holding it in the fashion condemned. Of the Lord of glory he observes that there is no word for Lord in the Greek at all, the phrase being simply the Glory and standing in apposition, so that James terms Christ the Shekinah Glory of God. The word for respect of persons he calls a Christian coinage, unknown in any previous Greek, made from the Hebrew idiom of lifting up the face on a person. Clarke would have the whole verse read interrogatively — do ye not make profession of the religion of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with acceptance of persons? — preferring the rich merely for their riches, and not for any moral excellence; faith here, he notes, stands for religion, and though the manuscripts vary the meaning is clear enough. Ellicott hears in the severity of the rebuke the apostle's consciousness of its need: what were endurable in a heathen ceased to be so in a follower of the lowly Jesus, who being rich became poor for our sakes. True reverence is not condemned, but its gross extreme — the preference for vulgar wealth, the adulation of success, the worship of some new golden calf. Wesley grounds the admonition on the name brethren itself, and Gill likewise, the saints being children of one Father; Barnes, opening the chapter, sets out its three parts — impartiality, obedience to the whole law, and the necessity of works to justification.
2:
The word James uses for the meeting arrests every commentator, this being the only place in the New Testament where synagogue is applied to a Christian congregation. Barnes supposes it employed because the apostle was writing to former Jews, among whom it would naturally be used of a Christian place of worship until superseded by a word the Gentile converts preferred. The one term refers to a congregation simply as assembled, without respect to whether all were truly pious; the other to an assembly called out, and so suited a body of spiritual worshippers better. The Christian church was probably modelled on the Jewish synagogue, but it was hard to avoid the associations of the name. Robertson adds the later evidence: Epiphanius states that the Ebionites called their church a synagogue, and a fourth-century inscription uses the word of a Christian meeting-house — though in James he takes it as another incidental argument for the early date. Clarke reads it more strictly, supposing the apostle addresses Jews who continued to frequent the synagogues to hear the law and the prophets read; our word assembly does not express the original. He inclines rather to proceedings in a court of justice, since petty courts were held in the synagogues, and thinks the case a judicial one in which the ruler deferred to the rich man and neglected the poor, though at law they were equal. Gill notes the same division.

The two men are drawn with some care. Ellicott renders the phrases a man golden-ringed in bright apparel, and observes that the Roman satirists had much to say of the fops of their time with all their fingers laden with rings, some, on Martial's sneer, having six on each; no doubt the fashions set in Rome reached Jerusalem. Goodly apparel he would render gorgeous, and the poor man's raiment squalid, even dirty, as from work and wear — the exact opposite of the idle over-dressed exquisite. Robertson calls the first word a gold-fingered man, occurring nowhere else in Greek, and quotes Vincent's illustration that Hannibal after Cannae sent to Carthage three bushels of gold rings from the fingers of slain Roman knights; the contrast, in Hort's phrase, is between new glossy clothes and old shabby ones. Barnes takes the ring as indicative of rank or property, common among the rich and those who desired to be esteemed rich, and thinks the reference is not to members of the church but to persons who might drop in to witness the service.

On the seating Barnes is careful to state what is not forbidden. Religion does not forbid proper respect to rank, office, age, or distinguished talents, nor a man's procuring himself an eligible pew if he has the means; but it requires that men be regarded according to their moral worth and not their external adorning, all being in fact on a level before God. The good place he takes to be an honourable seat near the pulpit, given merely from the indications of wealth and without knowing anything of the man's character; the poor man is not offered a seat at all. Ellicott presses harder: the elder in charge finds a stall for the person of substantial presence, while anything does for the poor one, who may stand or sit on the floor beneath the great man's feet. He asks what excuse can be urged for special pews hired and appropriated, furnished luxuriously and secured by bolt and lock, while the poorly clad are crowded into side benches. Clarke sees a judge prejudging the cause, giving the poor man to understand that he was to expect no impartial justice; Robertson notes that the preposition means down beside, as at a mountain's foot, and that conquerors often set their feet on the necks of their victims. Gill calls it an instance of the respect of persons condemned.
4:
Barnes finds two ideas in the charge, though it has been much disputed. The first is that by such conduct they took it upon themselves to be judges, pronouncing on strangers and their claims to respect; the second, that in doing so they were guided by no just rule, but by that improper feeling which honours men for their appearance rather than their real worth. Robertson renders the question, were ye not divided in yourselves? — guilty of a divided mind as between the two strangers — and notes that the word for reasoning is not necessarily evil, though the Gospels use it so. Clarke paraphrases it as making a distinction before the case has been heard, by judges who say in their hearts, we will espouse the cause of the rich because they can befriend us, and neglect the poor. Calvin allows the clause to be read as question or statement with the same sense: whether their own conscience does not hold them convicted, needing no other judge; or that they do not think they sin at all. Wesley puts it shortest — fine apparel is no proof of worth in him that wears it; and Gill, that the partiality was such as their own consciences must accuse them of.

Calvin finds two arguments against the preference of the rich. The first is that it is disgraceful to cast down those whom God exalts; since God honours the poor, everyone who repudiates them reverses the order of God. The second is from experience: the rich are for the most part vexatious to the good and innocent, so that it is unreasonable to reward their wrongs by approving them above the poor, who aid us more than they wrong us. God pours out his grace on rich and poor in common, yet his will is to prefer these to those — as Paul says that God has chosen not many noble, not many mighty, but the weak, to shame the strong — so that the mighty may learn not to flatter themselves. The rich in faith, Calvin adds, are not those who abound in the greatness of faith, but those whom God has enriched with the gifts of his Spirit, which we receive by faith; if we are empty that proves the deficiency of our faith, God being ready to fill the bosom of faith if we enlarge it.

The others take the choice more simply. Barnes says the meaning is not that God is less willing to save the rich, for he has no partiality, but that circumstances in the condition of the poor make it likelier they will embrace the gospel, and that the great mass of believers is in fact taken from those in humble life; that God has chosen a man to be an heir of the kingdom is as good a reason now why he should not be neglected as then. Robertson observes that by the article James does not affirm God chose all the poor, but only that he chose poor people, rich because of their faith. Clarke refers the words to our Lord's own sign, that the poor have the gospel preached to them: these believed while the rich persecuted him, and so were prized of God even while despised of men. Ellicott grants that there is an election here and that it were folly to deny it, but observes that the passage gives the reason for the choice — the poor are His chosen not merely for their poverty, though poverty may have been the air in which the virtues that endeared them flourished best. In a worship that demands costly gifts of its votaries, as every religion tends downward to do, the rich man has a golden pavement to his future bliss. Wesley asks: those whom God so highly honours, ought not we to honour likewise?
6:
Calvin meets an objection before it is raised. James seems to instigate them to vengeance by bringing forward the unjust rule of the rich, as though those unjustly treated might render like for like, whereas we are bid to do good to those who injure us. But his object was to show that they were without reason who through ambition honoured their executioners and meanwhile injured their own friends, from whom they had never suffered wrong. Their vanity appeared the more in this, that they admired the rich merely because they were rich, and flattered those whom they found, to their own loss, unjust and cruel. There are indeed some rich men who are just, but few; James mentions what daily experience proves, that as men commonly exercise power in doing wrong, the more power one has the worse he is towards his neighbours. Gill puts it more sharply: to reproach the poor is in effect to say that God did a weak or a wrong thing in choosing them to be heirs of a kingdom.

On the oppression itself Ellicott is fullest. The rich lord it over the poor as a class, which is not to say it of each wealthy man; it is the rich man of the earth earthy, trusting in his riches, who makes them a power for evil. The second charge he would render, do they not drag you into courts of justice — hale you, as the old English word has it — and sets against it the maxim that the extreme of right is the extreme of wrong, the purse-proud litigious man being the hardest to deal with and the readiest to grind the faces of the poor. No body of laws could be more equitable than the Roman, but their administration in the provinces was often in venal hands, and the fees of the learned in the law barred the way of poorer suitors, such as most of these Christians were. Clarke says the same of the Jewish courts, whose justice was then in a miserable state of corruption, so that a Christian might expect none anywhere but from his God. Robertson notes that the word for oppression is used of the devil in Acts, and that for dragging is an old and vigorous term for violence, used of Paul himself. Wesley distinguishes them neatly: the rich oppress by open violence, and drag under colour of law. Barnes adds that the meaning is not that they oppressed the poor as such, but those whom James addressed.

The last charge Barnes turns into a mirror. Those who persecuted Christians would revile the name they bore, and many who stopped short of persecution still spoke contemptuously of Christ. Yet many who profess to be Christians have been more disposed to treat such persons with respect than their own poorer brethren, cultivating their favour, aping their manners and coveting their society. Though such men are known to despise religion in their hearts, there is many a professing Christian who would rather be at a party given by them than at a prayer-meeting where his poorer brethren are assembled. Ellicott observes that to blaspheme is to hurt with the tongue and takes in all manner of evil speech, though the word is used more strictly of things divine, and that the name invoked over them was invoked at baptism; the scorn visited on that Name changed mere abuse into a perilous likeness to the deadliest sin. Robertson agrees that the beautiful name called upon them is almost certainly Christ's, and Calvin that it is the name of God and of Christ, called on them not in prayer but by profession. Clarke thinks these blasphemers plainly Jews, since no Christians of that early time could have acted the part described; Wesley thinks rather of rich heathens, but asks whether Christians, so called, are a whit behind them.
8:
Henry observes that a gospel ministry must not only reprove but teach, and that James now shows how the matter may be mended. Lest any think he had pleaded for the poor so as to throw contempt on the rich, he lets them know they must not be rude to the rich any more than despise the poor. The rule for Christians to walk by is settled in the scriptures — not great men, nor worldly wealth, nor the corrupt practices of professors, but the scriptures of truth must guide us. The law is royal because it comes from the King of kings, and because the state in which Christians now are is one of liberty and not of bondage. And a pretence of observing it, interpreted with partiality, will not excuse unjust proceedings: some would plead that respect to those whom providence had distinguished was but doing right. They did well, Henry allows, in giving honour to whom honour was due; but that fair pretence would not cover the sin charged.

Calvin reads the verse as an anticipation, meeting an excuse before it is offered. They might have objected that no one ought to be blamed who humbly submits to the unworthy; James concedes this in itself, but shows the plea falsely made, since they showed this homage not from love but from respect of persons. The hinge turns on the words neighbour and respect of persons: God bids us love our neighbours and not show respect of persons, and neighbour includes all mankind — so that he who says a very few, according to his own fancy, ought to be honoured and the rest passed by does not keep the law of God. God expressly commends to us strangers and enemies, to which respect of persons is wholly contrary. Of the epithet royal Calvin thinks it means the royal road, plain and level, set against sinuous by-paths; and he sees an allusion to the servile obedience they rendered the rich, when by serving their neighbours in sincerity they might be not merely free men but live as kings.

The others explain the epithet in their own ways. Clarke notes that of all the New Testament writers only James uses it, though it is frequent among the Greeks for anything of general concern, suitable and necessary to all, as brotherly love is. It is royal not only as proceeding from God's kingly authority, but because it is so necessary to the present state of man; and since it was given by Christ himself, who is our King as well as Prophet and Priest, it should put us in mind of his authority over us. Barnes takes it as kingly for its nobleness, having such prominence among laws as a king among men, and fit to govern all our intercourse as a king rules his subjects. Robertson recalls the Roman phrase for a law coming from the king, and allows the sense to be a law fit to guide a king, or such as a king would choose, or even the king of laws; since Jesus said that on the law of love hang all the law and the prophets, this is probably the royal law violated by partiality. Gill calls love to God the king of laws and love to the neighbour its queen, and notes that the same Hebrew word signifies princes and to be willing, so that this law is obeyed royally by such as are made kings and priests to God. Ellicott hears a touch of irony in the defence James puts into his hearers' mouths, the conduct described being a sweet proof of neighbourly affection indeed; yet the sovereign law of love is so plain that the simplest mind may be its interpreter. Wesley calls it the supreme law of the great King, which is love to every man, poor as well as rich.
9:
Barnes warns that convinced is not used here in its modern sense, of the impression made on a man's mind by showing him a truth he had doubted, as a man may be convinced he is a sinner and fall into the distress called conviction. Here it refers not to the effect on the mind but to the fact that the law holds such a one guilty. Robertson calls the charge serious for what was thought a trifling fault, recalling our Lord's words to those that work iniquity. Ellicott renders it that they are convicted at the bar of conscience: the first principle has been broken, not a mere detail. Calvin takes the law here in its proper meaning: since we are bidden to embrace all mortals, everyone who keeps a few exceptions and rejects the rest breaks the bond of God and inverts his order. Clarke says they are convicted by this royal law, having refused justice to the poor and upheld the rich; Gill, that this is no doing well but a transgression, as every sin is.

On the harder saying that follows, Calvin says what it does not mean. At first view it seems hard, as though the apostle countenanced the Stoic paradox that makes all sins equal, and held that he who offends in one thing should be punished as one whose whole life has been wicked; but the context shows no such thing entered his mind. What he means is that God will not be honoured with exceptions, nor allow us to cut from his law what is less pleasing. He denies that our neighbours are loved when a part only is chosen through ambition and the rest neglected, since obedience is no obedience when not rendered equally; as the rule of God is complete, none of us should separate what he has joined. Were a judge to punish ten thefts and leave one man unpunished, he would betray the obliquity of his mind, being indignant against men rather than crimes, since what he condemns in one he absolves in another. If we cut from God's law what is less agreeable, we become guilty of all, because in one particular we violate the whole. God has prescribed a rule of life which it is not lawful to mutilate, and promises a reward only to universal obedience; foolish, then, are the schoolmen who deem partial righteousness meritorious.

Clarke traces the form of speech to the rabbins. In one tract Rabbi Yochanan says that if a man do the whole with the omission of one, he is guilty of the whole and of every one; elsewhere an adulteress is shown by that one crime to break all ten commandments. But he also finds them teaching the reverse — that he who observed any principal command was equal to him who kept the whole law — and it is this false doctrine, he thinks, that James corrects here. Ellicott puts it in an image: as a chain is snapped by the weakest link, so the whole law, in its completeness as beheld by God, is broken by one offence of one man. Barnes draws it out at law: a man who has stolen a horse is a violator of the law however many other respects he has kept it in, and cannot urge his good citizenship to escape punishment. Robertson says the same more shortly: to be a lawbreaker one need not violate all the laws, but to be law-abiding one must keep them all. On the two commandments Calvin observes that the Lawgiver is to be considered rather than each precept apart, God's righteousness being contained in the law as an indivisible body; Robertson, that people free from fleshly sins have often made their condemnation of them an excuse for indulgence towards spiritual ones; and Wesley, that one authority establishes every commandment.
12:
Barnes explains the rule we are to be judged by. In all our conduct we are to act under the constant impression that we shall soon be judged, and by a law under which it was contemplated that we should be set free from the dominion of sin. We shall not be able to plead that we were under a necessity of sinning; and if we could have led holy lives, it is proper we be condemned if we are not righteous. He who habitually feels that he is soon to be judged by such a law has, Barnes thinks, the strongest inducement to lead a holy one. Ellicott notes that the term occurs only here and in the first chapter: it means neither the ceremonial law nor the moral, but the spiritual law of One greater than Moses. Robertson warns that it is law after all, not the caprice of personal liberty. Clarke and Wesley identify it with the gospel — the law of universal love, which alone is perfect freedom — and Gill adds that words as well as works transgress it.

Calvin reports one explanation but prefers another. Some say that men who flattered themselves are summoned here to the right tribunal, since they absolve themselves by their own notions when they withdraw from the divine law's judgment; and lest that smite them with terror, James adds the word liberty, meaning that we are freed from the law's rigour, whose judgment in itself is condemnation. That is not unsuitable, but a closer look at what follows shows he meant another thing. The sense is rather: except ye wish to undergo the rigour of the law, ye must be less rigid towards your neighbours, the law of liberty being the same as the mercy of God. So read with the verse after it the passage runs well — since none of us can stand before God unless delivered from the law's strict rigour, we ought so to act that we may not by severity shut out that indulgence of God which we all need to the last. God promises to be merciful to us if we are merciful to our brethren, not because our mercy merits his, but because he would have those he has adopted bear his image on earth; and all are lost who do not flee to the asylum of pardon.

On the closing sentence they differ over who triumphs. Calvin takes it that mercy itself in a manner triumphs and alone reigns when the severity of judgment gives way, and calls forced the explanation that puts mercy for the merciful man, since men cannot glory against the judgment of God. Clarke lists the readings without settling among them: that the merciful man exults over judgment, not being afraid of it; that we shall be exalted by mercy above judgment; and that in the great day God will cause mercy to triumph in bringing into glory those who fed the hungry. Barnes describes the triumph as a conflict of attributes: justice demands the sinner's condemnation, mercy pleads that he be saved, and mercy prevails — as with Major André, where Washington's justice was shown in the warrant he signed and his compassion in the tears he shed over it. Ellicott hears the clearest echoes of our Saviour's words and of the parable of the unmerciful servant, whose sin, he remarks, was the unforgiving temper apart from all outward wrong. He quotes a Greek father, that mercy is dear to God and intercedes for the sinner, breaks his chains and quenches the fire of hell, and stands by God's throne to plead for us when we are near condemnation. Robertson puts it in a line: only mercy can triumph over justice, with God and men alike. Wesley says the same: strict justice for the unmerciful, but for believers a mercy answering to what they have shown.
14:
Henry raises the great question at once — how to reconcile Paul and James — and answers it in three steps. First, when Paul says a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, he means another sort of work, though not another sort of faith: Paul, deeds wrought in obedience to Moses before men embraced the gospel; James, deeds done in obedience to the gospel as the necessary fruits of believing. Both magnify the same faith, the one by showing the insufficiency of legal works before it, the other by showing its genuine products. Second, the two address opposite errors: one had to do with men who leaned on their own merit, the other with men who cried up believing and disallowed obedience even as evidence. As we must not break one table of the decalogue against the other, so we must not shatter law and gospel by making them clash. Third, the justification differs — Paul speaks of our persons being acquitted before God, James of our faith being approved before men: our persons are justified before God by faith, our faith before men by works.

Wesley states the same case in his own way, and Clarke adopts his words entire. Since the exhortation to be doers of the word the apostle has been enforcing practice, and now turns on those who neglect it. Some had begun to wrest the doctrine of gratuitous justification to their own destruction; wherefore James, purposely repeating the same phrases and examples the apostle to the Gentiles had used, refutes not his teaching but the error of those who abused it. Both delivered the truth of God, but to different kinds of men. The point turns on a single word, for it is not though he have faith, but though he say he have it; nor does he oppose believing to obedience, but the empty name of the one to a living trust working by love. Clarke adds the history of the quarrel: Luther, supposing the doctrine here really to be salvation by merit, condemned the epistle outright as a chaffy thing, an epistle of straw fit only to be burnt.

Calvin fixes on the same word. A question arises whether faith can be severed from love, and this passage has produced the Sophists' distinction between unformed and formed faith; but of such a thing James knew nothing, for he does not begin, if any one has faith, but, if any says that he has it, intimating that hypocrites boast of an empty name which does not belong to them. That he calls it faith at all is a concession, as the rhetoricians say — in a dispute it does no harm, and is sometimes expedient, to grant an adversary what he demands, since once the thing itself is understood the grant may easily be withdrawn. We are not saved by a frigid and bare knowledge of God; salvation comes by faith because faith joins us to God, and that only by our being united to the body of Christ. There is nothing of this in the dead image: his meaning is, can the faith he says he has save him? Barnes marks the standpoint — not before a man is converted, inquiring on what ground his sins may be forgiven, but after, showing that a trust not followed by good living is not real. Robertson notes that the article is almost demonstrative, pointing back to the claim just made: it is the spurious pretension James condemns. Ellicott hears an allusion to the Shema, the devout Israelite's daily protest among idolaters, and thinks the stern question a prophecy of woe on a man who fancied himself saved by covenant. Gill notes the easy transition from partiality to this new subject, and Clarke that what is meant is a creed taking in no more than the being and unity of God.
15:
Barnes finds the comparison obvious and striking. Faith without the acts it would prompt is as cold and useless as it would be to say to one destitute of the necessaries of life, depart in peace. In the case of a man hungry or naked, what is wanted is not good wishes but the deeds to which they prompt; and so in religion what is wanted is not the abstract state of mind which faith indicates, but the life of goodness it ought to lead to. If we really have not the means of relieving the poor, a kind wish may itself alleviate their sorrow; but if we have the means, such expressions are mere mockery, and make deeper the sorrows we ought to heal. There is a great deal of that charity in the world, and much of the same kind of faith. That which is alive bodies itself forth; that which is dead is as if it were not. Clarke notes that naked here means ill-clothed, as elsewhere in the Gospels, and Ellicott that the food in question is that of each day, so that the case is one of the direst want, before which a heart untouched must be hard indeed.

Ellicott suspects the scene drawn from life — perhaps from the apostle's own experience during the famine foretold by Agabus. He finds a worse sense possible in the words, which begin so softly with the Eastern benediction: they may mean, ye are warming and filling yourselves — the rebuke of cool prosperity to importunate adversity, why such impatience, God is our Father, he will provide. No amount of faith could clothe the shivering limbs, and there is no greater mockery than to be taunted with texts and godly precepts, the usual outcome of a cheap benevolence. The one of you at the beginning stood for the whole body addressed, and by the change to the plural we see that no individual was singled out: the offence was wider. Robertson notes that go in peace is the common Jewish farewell, used by our Lord himself, and that the two imperatives are probably middle — warm yourselves, feed yourselves — so that instead of clothes and food they get only empty words: cold deeds with warm words. Clarke says such a saying will profit them just as much as a professed faith without works will profit the man who has it at the judgment.

On the verdict itself Calvin is exact. James says faith is dead when by itself, that is, destitute of good works, whence we conclude that it is no faith at all, since when dead it does not properly retain the name. The Sophists plead the expression and say that some sort of faith is found by itself; but the caviling is easily refuted, for the apostle reasons from what is impossible, as Paul calls an angel anathema if he should subvert the gospel. Ellicott renders it dead in its own self, and observes that if to be childless among women was a curse in Israel, so to be barren among God's graces is the condemnation of faith in Christendom. There had been no lack of charity under the earlier Jewish teaching, righteousness being often explained in the Targums as almsgiving; but rabbinism seems to have destroyed the spiritual life of its scholars, and a sterile faith was fast spreading among them. Gill likens such a faith to a lifeless carcass, a body without a soul, and adds from Dr Ames that good works are second acts, necessarily flowing from the life of faith, by which it appears to be living and active. Robertson calls it dead inwardly and outwardly, and Wesley a mere empty notion, of no more profit to him that has it than bidding the naked be clothed is to them.
18:
Who speaks here, and in what tone, divides the commentators. Robertson takes the opening particle as adversative and supposes James introduces an imaginary objector who speaks a single sentence, after which the apostle answers him; the objector may even be asking a short question, to which James replies that he has works too. Ellicott thinks the bearing of the verse commonly misunderstood: the words are those of scorn, uttered probably by some enemy of the faith, and the whole speech runs on to the argument about Abraham; yet whether the speaker be Christian or not, he lays claim to faith in God as the efficient cause of his good deeds. Calvin rejects the reading of Erasmus, who introduced two speakers, one boasting of faith without works and the other of works without faith; that seems too forced, its mistake being not to acknowledge an irony in the words. He would take the particle as nay rather, and read the whole as one speech: thou hast faith only, I have works besides; now prove that thou hast true faith without works, and I will prove mine by its fruits. The design was to expose those who imagined they had faith while their life showed them unbelievers.

Barnes reads it as an objection worth answering. It might be urged that religion is not always manifested in the same way, and that we should not suppose it absent because it does not take the same form: one man may be distinguished for zeal, another for meekness, another for benevolence, and all be religious men. The objection has some plausibility, and it was important to meet it. To this the apostle replies that the two are not independent qualities which can exist separately, but that the one is the germ of the other, and its existence is known only by its developing into the other. In proof of this he could appeal to anyone to show faith existing without works, and was himself willing to submit to that trial. Barnes reports the textual variation: many manuscripts read by thy works in the first clause as in the second, while without is found in others and in the Vulgate, and is now commonly received, being demanded by the later words about faith without works being dead.

Calvin adopts the same reading. James bids the boaster show faith without works, and so reasons from what is impossible, to prove what does not exist; if any prefer the other reading it comes to the same thing, the meaning either way being, unless thy faith brings forth fruits, I deny that thou hast any. This verse is for Calvin the key to the epistle. When James says a man is justified by works he means that a man is proved by his works to be justified, his faith being shown to be living and not dead; and it is a wonder that anyone surveying the whole passage should think there is any contrariety here to Paul, whose doctrine of justification by a living faith which works by love is perfectly consistent with it. He raises one further question, whether outward uprightness is a sure evidence of faith, and answers that the unbelieving sometimes excel in specious virtues and lead a life free from every crime, so that excellent works may exist apart from faith; James does not maintain that everyone who seems good possesses it, but only that faith without works is vainly pretended, since fruit ever comes from the living root of a good tree. Clarke says the same in a sentence: faith cannot be discerned but by its effects, so that he who has no good works has presumptively none, while works of charity show a living tree whose root is love to God and man. Gill makes the speaker a true believer calling on a vain boaster to give evidence of what he claims.
19:
Barnes explains why this doctrine is chosen. The apostle selects a cardinal truth, the belief of which would save the soul if belief in any doctrine could, and shows that even this may be held by those whom no one would call Christians. He is not addressing such a man as Paul, but one who held that provided there was faith a man would be saved; and he replies that the demons have a faith of a sort, which produces sensible effects, and still they are not saved. These spirits, Barnes observes, are never represented as denying God's existence — atheism is a sin of this world only. If such spirits may hold that faith and remain in perdition, men may hold it and go there too; a man should not infer that because he has a faith which fills him with alarm he is therefore safe.

On the word for their trembling the commentators pause. Barnes notes that it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means to be rough with bristling hair, to stand on end as the hair does in a fright — showing that there was much more here than a speculative faith, since this one produced a very decided effect, though not a holy life. Robertson calls it an onomatopoetic verb, like the Latin horror, and adds that the demons do more than believe a fact: they shudder at it. Ellicott renders the first clause thou believest that God is One, and grants the man his correctness — he is theologically right and may even confess it outwardly — but adds that assent, opinion and knowledge are shared by the demons of the pit, and that we should not call our joint possession with them by the holier name of faith. Clarke says belief in the being and unity of God distinguished these men from all the nations, and having been circumcised they thought themselves secure; but the same truth, far from saving the devils, leaves them damned, every act of believing it only increasing their torment, since they can neither love nor obey. Wesley allows the creed and denies the inference: this proves only that thou hast the same faith with the devils, who not only believe but tremble.

Calvin draws a sharper conclusion. From this one sentence it is evident that the whole dispute is not about faith at all, but about the common knowledge of God, which can no more connect a man with God than the sight of the sun can carry him to heaven, whereas by faith we come nigh to God; and it would be ridiculous to say that the devils have faith. James even prefers them to hypocrites, for the devil trembles at the mention of God's name, acknowledging his judge, so that he who despises an acknowledged God is much worse — the words being added by way of extenuation, as though it were a great thing, forsooth, to sink below the devils. Of the reproach that follows, Calvin insists we must understand the state of the question: the dispute is not about the cause of justification but about what a profession of faith without works avails; absurdly then do they act who prove from this passage that man is justified by works. Barnes takes the epithet as empty, void of understanding, and a mild way of calling a man foolish — if we must do so, let us use a term which conveys our meaning without needlessly wounding. Robertson notes that some copies read barren, or rather inactive, like land with no crops. Ellicott quotes Beveridge, that as the fruit tells what the tree is, so a man's life tells how he believes. Gill thinks the epithet levelled at the Gnostics, empty vessels making the greatest sound; Wesley, that such a faith is not faith at all, as a dead carcase is not a man.
21:
Calvin says the Sophists lay hold on the one word and cry out as victors that justification is partly by merit, but we ought to seek a right interpretation from the drift of the whole passage. James does not speak of the cause of justification, nor of how men obtain righteousness, but only shows that good deeds always accompany believing; and in calling Abraham justified he speaks of the proof the patriarch gave of it. When the Sophists set James against Paul they go astray through the ambiguity of a term: Paul means the gratuitous imputation of righteousness before the tribunal of God, James its manifestation by conduct before men, as the preceding words about showing faith make plain. In this latter sense we fully allow that a man is justified by works — as one may say a man is enriched by the purchase of a large and valuable chest, because his riches, before shut up in it, were thus made known. Calvin adds that the difficulty vanishes as soon as we survey the whole passage instead of single expressions.

Robertson concedes that this is the phrase often held flatly opposed to Paul, who says pointedly that it was the patriarch's believing and not his doing that was reckoned to him for righteousness; but Paul speaks of what Abraham had before his circumcision. The two use the same words of different acts: James points to the offering of Isaac as the fruit of a trust already held, Paul discusses that trust as the ground of acquittal, so that neither answers the other. Wesley fixes the distinction by dates — the one speaks of an acquittal received many years before Isaac was born, the other of one not received till the boy was laid on the altar; so that the second justification is the fruit of the first. Barnes adds that the apostle cannot mean justification in the ordinary sense, since the very passage he quotes makes Abraham's acceptance consequent on his believing, whereas this act came long afterwards and confirmed it. Ellicott notes that Isaac was a type of God's dear Son, who bore, like his meek ancestor, the sacrificial wood up the road of death; and Clarke asks whether the patriarch's conduct did not sufficiently prove what led him to so extraordinary an act.

On the co-operation, Barnes explains the word as contributing to a result which two agents jointly produce. What Abraham reached was not secured by one alone; and though the apostle says nothing of the merit of each, he looks at the outcome as it appeared under trial, where the two are plainly seen working together. That it was made perfect does not mean it had been defective and the defect remedied, but that it was so carried out as to show its legitimate results — the completeness a thing has when fully developed. Calvin reports the difficulty of rendering the verb, which properly means to work together and so to aid: some read that faith aided Abraham in his obedience, others that it combined with it in justification. He prefers the first: faith is perfected by obedience not because it takes its perfection thence, but because it is thus proved true. The Sophists' distinction between formed and unformed faith needs no refutation, since Abraham's was perfected before he sacrificed his son, and this was not the last of his trials, others following by which he proved its increase. Clarke says that even a true faith will soon die if its possessor do not live in the spirit of obedience; Wesley, that believing begets deeds and is then perfected by them, as the natural heat of the body begets motion, whereby itself is increased. Gill notes that a true faith will engage a man to do good, as it did Abraham; Ellicott would take the opening clause simply, not as a question.
23:
Calvin will not let the quotation be turned round. Those who prove from it that Abraham's obedience was imputed for righteousness must confess that Scripture is perverted by them, for however they twist they can never make the effect its own cause. The imputation Moses mentions preceded by more than thirty years the deed by which they would have the patriarch justified — it was reckoned to him fifteen years before Isaac was born, so that it can hardly have been done through the sacrificing of a son who did not yet exist. All are bound fast by an indissoluble knot who imagine righteousness imputed because he offered Isaac, when the Spirit had declared him justified before the boy's birth. Why then speak of fulfilment? Because he intended to show what sort of faith justified Abraham — not idle or evanescent, but such as rendered him obedient to God. The conclusion that follows depends on this: a man is not justified by faith alone, that is, by a bare knowledge of God, but by works, that is, his righteousness is known and proved by its fruits.

Barnes sets out the same chronology from the other side. What Abraham believed was the promise that his heir should be one out of his own bowels and his seed as the stars for number; the act of confiding in it was what was counted to him for righteousness. The offering on the altar came twenty years later and confirmed it — for what could confirm it more than a readiness to give up his own son at God's command? It cannot be supposed that James meant Abraham was justified without respect to faith, since the very passage he quotes shows faith first; the meaning is that the declaration received its full expression when, long afterwards, a striking act of obedience showed it to be real. Robertson observes that James quotes the same verse Paul does to prove that Abraham's believing preceded his circumcision, and that both are right, each illustrating a different point. Clarke puts it shortest: he believed God, and this faith was never inactive; his obedience showed that he had not received the grace of God in vain. Wesley says the word was twice fulfilled, when Abraham first believed and when he offered Isaac, Paul speaking of the former and James of the latter.

The title given him draws comment of its own. Barnes calls it a most honourable appellation, granted for strong faith and obedience. Clarke calls it the highest character ever given to man, and reasons from the nature of friendship: as among friends everything is in common, so, God never being in want, his friend could never be destitute. Ellicott corrects a common mistake about the phrase — it means beloved of God, not the friend to God — and adds that it is no exact quotation from the Hebrew, and that the term was traditional throughout the East, used by the Arabs of the patriarch to this day; Robertson notes that Philo uses it too. On the conclusion drawn from the whole, Ellicott observes that the adverb stands last and most emphatic: James never denies justification by faith, but only that fancied one by an idle faith with no corresponding acts of love. Robertson agrees that the phrase clears up his meaning: a live faith is what we must all have, only it must show itself in deeds as Abraham's did. Barnes states the doctrine plainly: the ground of justification is faith and that only, the evidence is good works, and so James contradicts not Paul but a false explanation of him. Wesley distinguishes both terms — one apostle speaks of a living faith and the other of a dead one, one of works antecedent and the other of works subsequent. Gill adds that good works do not precede justification as causes, but follow as fruits.
25:
Calvin thinks the pairing strange, and finds the reason in it. Why did the apostle not choose one from the large number of illustrious fathers to set beside Abraham, and why prefer a harlot to all others? He designedly put together two persons so different in character in order to show that no one, whatever his condition, nation or class in society, has ever been counted righteous without good works. Having named the patriarch, the most eminent of all, he now includes under the person of a harlot all those aliens who were joined to the Church; so that whoever seeks to be counted righteous, though among the lowest, must show it by his living. Calvin grants that James declares Rahab justified by works, and that the Sophists conclude we obtain righteousness by merit; but he denies that the dispute is about the mode of obtaining righteousness at all. We allow that good works are required for righteousness; we only take from them the power of conferring it, since they cannot stand before the tribunal of God. Wesley reads the pairing the same way: after Abraham, father of the Jews, the apostle cites a woman and a sinner of the Gentiles, to show that in every nation and sex a true faith produces works.

Ellicott dwells on the contrast and refuses to soften it. The second example stands in complete contrast to the father of many nations: Rahab, who sheltered in her house at Jericho the two spies sent from the camp of Israel. The evil name of the poor woman's unhappy trade cannot truthfully be softened to innkeeper, nor even to idolater. The verb rendered sent them out means literally thrust them forth, showing her haste and fear. He notes that Clement of Rome sees in the scarlet thread she bound in her window a type of our Redeemer's blood; and it is most remarkable, as showing the mercy of God, that this outcast was not only brought into the fold of Israel but became a direct ancestress of her Saviour by marriage with Salmon. Robertson observes that her vicious life she left behind, but the name clung to her always; the word for the men she received means messengers, where the Epistle to the Hebrews calls them spies, and the other way she sent them was through a window instead of a door.

Barnes marks the limits of the commendation. She is justified in the same sense Abraham was, showing by her act that her faith was genuine and no cold assent; had the act not been performed, that would have shown her faith unreal, but God saw it as it was and accepted her. We are not to suppose, however, that everything in her life and character is commended. She is commended for her faith and the fair expression of it — a faith which, as it led her to receive the messengers of the true God and to join herself to his people, we may suppose also induced her to abandon her former course. Clarke observes that justification signifies not only pardon but the receiving of divine approbation, and that James seems to use it in this latter sense, since God approved these two for their obedience, and approves no man who is not obedient. Gill draws the general rule: wherever there is true faith, in Jew or Gentile, man or woman, greater or lesser sinners, there will be good works — and he is a vain man who boasts of his faith while slighting them. Calvin, glancing ahead to the closing simile, warns against pressing it too far: the meaning is not that works are to faith what the spirit is to the body, which would make works the life of faith — the reverse of the fact — but that a faith having no works is like a dead carcass.
26:
The closing simile is plain enough in itself. Barnes takes the word for spirit in its common sense of the soul: the body is kept alive by its presence and has no life apart from it, so there is as much necessity that faith and works be united to make true religion as that body and soul be united to make a living man. If faith produces no fruit of good living, that proves it dead. This shows, he adds, that James was not arguing against real faith nor against its importance in justification, but against the supposition that mere faith was all that was necessary. Robertson observes that the word means apart from breath, and that it is not easy to tell when a man is dead, though the absence of any breath on a glass held before the mouth is proof of it — a startling picture, he says, of church members with only a name to live. Gill notes that the Jews say the same, calling a body without breath a carcass.

Ellicott, however, thinks the terms of the comparison are not what we should expect. Of our own human wisdom we had been rather inclined to say that works were likest the body and faith the breath of it; and he quotes Alford's account of the apostle's view — that faith is the body, the sum and substance of the Christian life, and works the quickening of that body, just as the spirit quickens the natural one. He notes too that the preposition rendered without is hardly strong enough, and should rather be apart from. Clarke draws the moral out at length: there can no more be a genuine faith without good works than a living body without a soul, and we shall never find disinterested godly living without true faith, nor true faith without such a life. We may see works of apparent benevolence without faith, but their principle is ostentation, and they last only while they have the reward of human applause. Where true faith is, there is God: his Spirit gives life and his love affords motives to righteous actions, and the use of any divine principle leads to its increase — the more a man exercises faith the more he is enabled to believe, and the more able to work for God.

Both Clarke and Barnes close by looking back over the whole dispute. Clarke quotes Michaelis, that some persons known to James must have taught that men are justified by merely believing in one true God, or he would not have taken such pains to confute it; and in denying that faith any avail unaccompanied by good works he has said nothing more than Paul says elsewhere against the same error, that not the hearers but the doers of the law will be justified. Barnes appends a formal reconciliation, observing first what the difficulty is: James seems to contradict Paul in express terms, and both use the same case to illustrate opposite sentiments. He recalls that infidels, and Voltaire in particular, seized on what they supposed they had found here to pronounce the Scriptures contradictory; and that Luther felt the difficulty so great that early in his career he denied the inspiration of the epistle, though he afterwards changed his opinion, while one of his followers was so displeased as to charge the writer with wilful falsehood. The question, he says, is whether their statements can be reconciled so that both may be regarded as inspired — and his answer, drawn out through the chapter, is that Paul speaks of the ground of justification and James of its evidence, both requiring a faith which produces a holy life; unless ours is of that kind it has no more of true religion in it than a dead body has of a living man.
